title: Primarily static circuit design style
decision: Adopt a predominantly complementary static-circuit design strategy, with dynamic circuits used only sparingly in SRAMs, register files, and a few critical core regions.
alternatives_or_rejected: Widespread use of dynamic logic for speed (common in high-frequency designs of the era).
rationale: Power dissipation was a major concern; SOI floating-body uncertainties affected noise immunity and decoupling needs; the chip’s size and logical complexity, plus schedule risk and design-team skill mix, favored a simple, robust style that minimized CAD and verification risk and eased future technology migration.
outcome: Overall logic was >99 % static outside arrays; the approach supported meeting frequency, power, and schedule goals with manageable noise and testability (LSSD-compatible latches).

title: Global slew-rate limit of one-third cycle time
decision: Enforce a global slew-rate limit equal to one-third of the cycle time for every signal (local and global) across the entire chip.
alternatives_or_rejected: Allowing faster slews on critical nets or leaving slew unconstrained beyond local checks.
rationale: To ensure a robust design that minimizes coupled-noise impact on timing and reduces sensitivity of path delay to wiring-process variability and device-model uncertainty.
outcome: Approximately 100 000 buffers/inverters were inserted to satisfy the limit; the rule was treated as part of the cycle-time budget and contributed to predictable timing closure.

title: Single chip-wide global clock domain without skew feedback
decision: Use a single chip-wide global clock domain driven by an SOI-optimized PLL and a tuned tree-plus-grid network, with no skew-feedback or adjustable delay settings.
alternatives_or_rejected: Multiple clock domains or active skew-adjustment circuitry to compensate for residual skew.
rationale: Simplifies timing methodology and enables rapid bring-up; prior server-microprocessor experience showed that a carefully tuned passive distribution could meet targets without feedback complexity on this size of chip.
outcome: Measured skew of ~20 ps and jitter of ~35 ps; “correct-by-design” clock that required no post-silicon adjustment and supported the >1.3 GHz target.

title: Selective, late-binding use of low-Vt devices
decision: Use reduced-Vt devices only in the most timing-critical paths, keeping total low-Vt usage under ~10 % of logic transistors; technology allowed last-minute Vt swaps with minimal layout change.
alternatives_or_rejected: Broad or early application of low-Vt transistors across large logic regions.
rationale: Low-Vt devices gave ~10 % performance gain but increased off-state leakage; selective use captured the speed benefit while avoiding a large standby-current penalty.
outcome: Performance targets met without a prohibitive leakage increase; Vt decisions could be postponed until late in the design cycle.

title: On-chip decoupling capacitance budgeting for transient IR
decision: Embed ~250 nF of decoupling capacitance in critical areas, sized from transient chip/package analysis to keep supply fluctuations under 10 % for a ~25 W maximum power step (chip power ~115 W).
alternatives_or_rejected: Relying primarily on package-level decoupling or a smaller on-chip budget.
rationale: Transient analyses showed that the resonant package/chip response to abrupt power changes required this on-chip capacitance to hold voltage within limits; average IR was separately constrained to <30 mV.
outcome: Supply integrity targets were met; white-space fill combined decoupling cells with gate-array backfill for late metal-only logic fixes.
